{"id": "53:5/q03", "question": "Who is 'the one mighty in powers' who taught?", "turns_on": "Whether the surrounding angelic descriptions and vision language point to Gabriel, or God's own teaching in 55:1-2 is the immediate sense; Qashani gives a spiritual designation.", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q03/p1", "position": "Gabriel, God's angel and messenger of revelation.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls him powerful in every respect; Farra connects dhu mirra in the next verse. Mawardi asserts consensus, Qurtubi a majority, and Ibn Ashur unanimity among exegetes; Ibn Abbas, Qatada, and al-Rabi are repeatedly cited. Ibn Atiyya says the following descriptions fit Gabriel and argues from 53:13's 'another descent' and the absence of a report of seeing God before the Night Journey, while allowing heart-sight of God; Abu Hayyan calls the God reading far-fetched. Samin finds Gabriel most apparent; Ibn Kathir compares 81:19-21, Tabatabai 81:20. Baydawi and Elmalili call Gabriel the intermediary of miracles; Aisha's report names him. Kuranyolu favors him from the flow and description; Samarrai says the wording identifies Gabriel as the revealer beyond ordinary ilham. Biqai links his extraordinary capacity to the unlettered Prophet's instruction. Farra, Ibn Qutayba, Zajjaj, and others identify him directly."}, {"id": "53:5/q03/p2", "position": "God is the mighty teacher.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan is cited by Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, and Abu Hayyan; Elmalili cites a report from Ibn Abbas; Tabatabai and Study Quran report the view. Samin adduces 55:1-2 as its support. Abu Hayyan finds it far-fetched, and Ibn Atiyya argues the continuation and 53:13 favor Gabriel, while allowing a vision of God by the heart."}, {"id": "53:5/q03/p3", "position": "The Spirit of Holiness, a spirit powerful over the levels beneath it, taught him.", "reasons": "Qashani describes its power to subdue and affect lower levels; he does not name it Gabriel in this note."}]}
{"id": "53:5/q04", "question": "What does 'mighty' say about the teacher's power?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase emphasizes intrinsic faculties or the means at the teacher's disposal; the notes offer no explicit argument against either gloss.", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q04/p1", "position": "His capacities are exceptionally strong, including the ability to execute divine commands and preserve revelation.", "reasons": "Muqatil says powerful in every respect; Tabrisī says Gabriel is powerful in himself and his created form. Razi describes strong intellectual and practical faculties and specifically perception, memory, and integrity, comparing the strong and trustworthy messenger of 81:20-21. Nishaburi gives the intellectual and practical reading. Ibn Ashur includes great intellectual and physical works and bringing revelation to messengers. Biqai says he can carry out all God's commands. Samarrai joins strength with knowledge, judgment, and precision for ascent, protection of the Prophet, and preservation of revelation, citing the need for sultan in 55:33."}, {"id": "53:5/q04/p2", "position": "He is strong in means or resources.", "reasons": "Elmalili attributes this gloss to Tabari."}]}
{"id": "53:5/q05", "question": "How is Gabriel's strength illustrated in transmitted accounts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q05/p1", "position": "Accounts point to his overwhelming acts and extraordinarily swift movement.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi in Tha'labi and Qurtubi says Gabriel lifted Lot's towns from black water on his wing and overturned them; Qurtubi says he carried them to heaven. Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi, and Alusi repeat the Lot account with variants of subterranean or dark water and raising to heaven. Al-Kalbi says a wing stroke threw Iblis to a distant Indian mountain; Qurtubi places the encounter during Iblis's speech to Jesus, while Bursevi says the blast sent him from the Holy Land to India. Al-Kalbi also cites Gabriel's cry killing Thamud; Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursevi, and Alusi repeat it, with Baydawi saying they lay collapsed by morning. Al-Kalbi describes rapid descents to prophets and ascents to heaven; Qurtubi says faster than a glance, and Alusi says faster than a blink, exceeding sunlight's speed."}]}
{"id": "53:5/q06", "question": "What does 'al-quwā' mean?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish inherent strength or ability from means or resources, without presenting a direct dispute.", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q06/p1", "position": "Strength, power, or capacity.", "reasons": "Majaz treats it as a collective for strength; Jishumi and Tabrisī gloss quwwa as ability rooted in strength. Ibn Qutayba traces its image to rope strands, one quwwa being a strand, as reported also by Ibn Jawzi. Bagḥawi and Ibn Atiyya call it plural of quwwa; Tabrisī and Bursevi compare mirra's image of a tightly twisted cord, with Bursevi citing Raghib and dictionary senses of physical strength, sound judgment, firmness, and strong rope. Razi and Nishaburi apply it to intellectual and practical powers."}, {"id": "53:5/q06/p2", "position": "Means or resources.", "reasons": "Elmalili cites Tabari's gloss of 'strong in powers' as strong in means or resources."}]}
{"id": "53:5/q07", "question": "What is the form of 'al-quwā'?", "turns_on": "Whether its form is explained as a plural of quwwa or as a collective expression.", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q07/p1", "position": "It is the plural of quwwa.", "reasons": "Akhfash compares dialectal plural pairs ḥabwa/ḥuban and rashwa/rashan; Ibn Qutayba and Ibn Jawzi use a rope strand as the singular image. Bagḥawi, Ibn Atiyya, and Tabrisī state the plural analysis."}, {"id": "53:5/q07/p2", "position": "It functions as a collective word for strength.", "reasons": "Majaz calls al-quwā a collective term."}]}
{"id": "53:5/q08", "question": "What variant reading of 'al-quwā' is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q08/p1", "position": "The qāf is read with kasra.", "reasons": "Nahhas attributes the reading to al-Farra, who grounds it in similarity between the patterns fiʿla and fuʿla."}]}
{"id": "53:5/q09", "question": "How is the phrase 'shadīd al-quwā' constructed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q09/p1", "position": "Shadīd is an intensive adjective annexed to its agent in a non-genuine construct; an implied 'angel' may be supplied.", "reasons": "Nasafi calls the genitive a construction of an intensive adjective with its agent, not true possession. {"id": "53:5/q10", "question": "Why describe the teacher as mighty in powers?", "turns_on": "The notes give complementary rhetorical purposes: student praise, rebuttal and assurance, and consolation.", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q10/p1", "position": "Praise of the teacher highlights the distinction and reliable instruction of Muhammad, his student.", "reasons": "Razi says praising Gabriel also praises Muhammad rather than merely naming the teacher; Nishaburi as cited by Elmalili and some exegetes as cited by Kuranyolu make the same point. Biqai says the extraordinary teacher makes the unlettered Prophet's instruction remarkable. Islahi portrays an affectionate teacher approaching and bending over his pupil so the Prophet fully grasped the teaching rather than hearing vague distant words."}, {"id": "53:5/q10/p2", "position": "It rebuts the claim that a weak human taught Muhammad, and establishes the revelation's dependable source.", "reasons": "Razi cites the opponents' claim that Muhammad heard ancient tales on a Syria trip, and compares Gabriel's perception, memory, and integrity with 81:20-21. Nishaburi contrasts humans' weakness and limited knowledge, citing 16:103, 4:28, and 17:85. Kuranyolu cites the unbelievers' human-teacher claim of 16:103. Samarrai says the wording identifies Gabriel rather than ordinary ilham such as that to Moses' mother, the bee, or humans and jinn. Islahi says 53:1-18 rejects soothsaying and fortune-telling by tracing the Qur'an to God's trusted angel."}, {"id": "53:5/q10/p3", "position": "The description consoles Muhammad by showing that Gabriel can bear divine communication.", "reasons": "Razi adds that God may teach first through an intermediary and then directly, citing 'He taught you what you did not know' in 4:113."}]}
{"id": "53:5/q11", "question": "How does Gabriel's teaching relate to God's teaching?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q11/p1", "position": "God is the ultimate teacher; Gabriel conveys the revelation by God's permission.", "reasons": "Elmalili cites 55:1-2 for God's teaching, 2:97, 16:102, 26:193, and 42:51 for Gabriel as messenger to Muhammad's heart. {"id": "53:5/q14", "question": "Whom did Muhammad see in the opening vision?", "turns_on": "Whether the descriptions and 53:13's 'another descent' identify Gabriel, or the passage describes a vision of God at the Night Journey; the mode of seeing God also varies.", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q14/p1", "position": "He saw Gabriel in his true form, unlike Gabriel's usual human appearance.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya favors Gabriel throughout these descriptions: 53:13 calls another descent, implying an earlier one, and no report places a sight of God before the Night Journey. {"id": "53:5/q15", "question": "What distinct reports describe a sight of Gabriel near this passage?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different vision scenes and details; the Anas account also has explicit transmission and wording objections.", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q15/p1", "position": "Anas reports that Gabriel struck the Prophet's shoulders and they rose from a tree to the horizons before a heavenly light, pearl-and-ruby veil, and revelation appeared.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir transmits Anas's account; Ibn Kathir calls it extraordinary, with objectionable wording, and suggests it may have been a dream. {"id": "53:5/q16", "question": "How is the Anas vision report assessed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q16/p1", "position": "Al-Harith ibn Ubayd was the sole transmitter, a known Basran, but the report has serious reliability objections.", "reasons": "Al-Bazzar identifies al-Harith as sole transmitter. {"id": "53:5/q17", "question": "How are the endings of the surrounding verses read?", "turns_on": "Which readers or transmissions use plain fatḥa, intermediate pronunciation, or imāla at particular endings.", "positions": [{"id": "53:5/q17/p1", "position": "Ibn Kathir, Asim, and Ibn Amir use fatḥa at all verse endings.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya transmits these assignments."}, {"id": "53:5/q17/p2", "position": "Asim through Abu Bakr uses imāla on raʾā.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya transmits this exception."}, {"id": "53:5/q17/p3", "position": "Nafi and Abu Amr use an intermediate form.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya transmits this assignment."}, {"id": "53:5/q17/p4", "position": "Hamza and al-Kisai use imāla throughout.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya transmits this assignment."}, {"id": "53:5/q17/p5", "position": "Abu Amr through Ubayd uses imāla for al-aʿlā and tadallā.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya transmits this exception."}]}
{"id": "53:10/q01", "question": "What does waḥy mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is defined by its communicative function, by speech in this context, or by other Arabic usages.", "positions": [{"id": "53:10/q01/p1", "position": "A swift, private communication of meaning by indication or speech.", "reasons": "Jishumi defines it as private conveyance to the mind. Ibn Qutayba and Ibn Faris, as cited by Ibn al-Jawzi, allow writing, gesture, message, or any means that makes another know; an unnamed definition stresses the swiftest and gentlest delivery. Al-Qurtubi cites the Arabic expression waḥāʾ waḥāʾ for swift casting."}, {"id": "53:10/q01/p2", "position": "Speech.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi glosses the word in this context as speech."}, {"id": "53:10/q01/p3", "position": "It can also denote swiftness or sound.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi cites istawḥaynāhum in the sense of calling them to cry out."}]}
{"id": "53:10/q02", "question": "Who reveals to whom in فَأَوْحَىٰٓ إِلَىٰ عَبْدِهِۦ?", "turns_on": "The understood subject, the recipient called 'His servant,' the pronouns' antecedents, and whether the preceding scene continues with Gabriel or shifts to God.", "positions": [{"id": "53:10/q02/p1", "position": "God reveals to His servant Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas is transmitted by al-Tabari, al-Nahhas, and Abu Hayyan; Muqatil, Ibn Qutayba, al-Thaʿlabi, al-Qushayri, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Samin, Ibn Ashur and others hold this subject and recipient. Al-Samin and Ibn Ashur say God is understood without an explicit prior name; Ibn Ashur cites 53:4. Al-Razi allows divine address or God creating necessary knowledge in Muhammad. Ibn Kathir accepts this along with Gabriel as subject. Elmalılı, al-Tabatabai and Kur'an Yolu favor this reading in the ascent setting, with direct revelation; al-Biqaʿi prefers the divine approacher in a cited report. Al-Tabatabai records a reading with all three pronouns referring to God; al-Baydawi and al-Biqaʿi also report all earlier pronouns as divine, al-Baydawi citing 51:58."}, {"id": "53:10/q02/p2", "position": "Gabriel reveals to God's servant Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Farra places Gabriel within two bow lengths of Muhammad; al-Tabari prefers continuity with the sura's earlier account of Muhammad and Gabriel, and al-Nahhas uses the surrounding narrative likewise. Al-Hasan, al-Rabiʿ, Ibn Zayd, Qatada, Ibn Abbas via Ata, and others transmit the reading, often saying Gabriel passes on what God revealed to him. Al-Wahidi says al-Farra, al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari chose it. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi allow the pronoun before Muhammad's explicit name because he is known; al-Nasafi compares 'what it left on its back.' Al-Alusi favors Gabriel as subject of both verbs over Abu Zayd's mixed subjects; Elmalılı says Gabriel's true-form appearance authenticated the source before piecemeal delivery. Ibn Kathir accepts this reading too."}, {"id": "53:10/q02/p3", "position": "God reveals to His servant Gabriel, who then conveys the message to Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan is reported by al-Tabari and, with Aisha and Qatada, by al-Mawardi. Ibn Abbas is reported by Ibn Atiyya. Al-Razi reads this as giving Gabriel proof that the message to Muhammad is revelation, distinguishing an angel from a jinn; he takes mā as a verbal noun. Al-Alusi calls the reading implausible."}]}
{"id": "53:10/q03", "question": "How is God's part in the communication related to Gabriel's?", "turns_on": "Whether the encounter is the direct Miʿraj communication or Gabriel's delivery of God's revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "53:10/q03/p1", "position": "God speaks directly to Muhammad without Gabriel as intermediary.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar in al-Sulami describes direct speech to Muhammad's heart and innermost secret, excepting the later grant of intercession. {"id": "53:10/q09", "question": "What do reports about the vision and divine disclosure add to this scene?", "turns_on": "The reports supply distinct visions, contents, and assessments of transmission.", "positions": [{"id": "53:10/q09/p1", "position": "A divine disclosure in a vision of the Highest Assembly's dispute.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas describes a vision, probably in sleep, in which God put a hand between Muhammad's shoulders and granted knowledge of heaven and earth. {"id": "53:10/q13", "question": "How do reports explain takbīr around al-Ḍuḥā and al-Sharḥ?", "turns_on": "Which occasion or liturgical function the takbīr marks.", "positions": [{"id": "53:10/q13/p1", "position": "It expressed the Prophet's distress over his household's fate.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi transmits from Ibn Abbas that the prospect of a household member entering Hell prompted takbir."}, {"id": "53:10/q13/p2", "position": "It referred to the Prophet's intercession.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan and Abu Jaʿfar al-Baqir give this explanation."}, {"id": "53:10/q13/p3", "position": "It marked the momentous or frightening vision of Gabriel.", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq says Gabriel revealed the sura in original form at al-Abtah; al-Nashr favors this because takbir usually responds to something momentous or frightening."}, {"id": "53:10/q13/p4", "position": "It honors God and marks grateful completion of recitation or blessing.", "reasons": "Makki gives this explanation and Ali's instruction to say takbir at the end of the Mufassal supports it. {"id": "53:13/q05", "question": "How is 'nazlatan' parsed?", "turns_on": "How an accusative noun naming one descent relates syntactically to the seeing verb.", "positions": [{"id": "53:13/q05/p1", "position": "An accusative adverbial of time or occasion.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari treats a noun of one occurrence as an adverb; al-Samin identifies this as al-Farra's school rather than the Basrans'.
